queue.goal: Turn Relay's production primitives into a durable resumable operation framework so agents invoke policy-defined workflows instead of manually conducting every GitHub, Cloudflare, Runner and QA step.
queue.acceptance: Every substantial workflow can create a stable operation_id with persisted stage/state, exact source/head/PR/check/merge/version/deployment/runtime identities, timestamps, retry/reconciliation history, blocker/waiting-for-human state and recovery/rollback state; reconnecting agents can resume from the durable receipt without reconstructing chat history; server-side recipes cover at least ship-change, publish-worker, qa-then-merge and rollback-release; ambiguous mutations reconcile by readback before retry; event/webhook updates can advance operation state without chat polling; release policy supports bounded canary/verify/promote/rollback semantics without protection bypass; operation status/history is queryable for UI; tool-surface growth stays minimal by preferring recipes/resources/contracts over one tool per step. Tool-pattern contract: operation recipes and their exposed tool interfaces consume the Relay 1.9.8 tool-design standard derived from Arcade's Agentic Tool Patterns. Recipes should prefer explicit task bundles/tool chains over forcing agents to manually orchestrate repetitive low-level calls, expose durable operation IDs and progressive status, classify failures with retry/user/auth/permanent semantics plus recovery guidance, preserve idempotent/readback/transaction boundaries, keep outputs structured/token-efficient, and enforce permission/secret/scope rules server-side. Deviations from applicable patterns must be explicit and justified; do not multiply tools merely to satisfy a pattern mechanically.
queue.next_action: Define the operation/receipt schema and transition invariants first, but consume the Relay 1.9.8 agentic-tool standard for recipe/tool boundaries, errors, discovery, output shaping and security. Reuse existing source/cloud/verify primitives and prefer durable high-level recipes where they eliminate fragile manual tool chains.

queue.goal: Expose Relay's MCP App dashboard as a first-class authenticated web dashboard on relay.loew.fi with parity to the in-chat state model and controls.
queue.acceptance: relay.loew.fi presents the same projects, durable operations, publication receipts, QA handoffs, release state, recovery/rollback actions and history as the MCP App without duplicating state; shared components/data adapters are reused where practical; deep links can open a specific project/operation/release/QA item; auth and mutations use Relay's existing bounded control plane; web and in-chat surfaces remain behaviorally consistent; the dashboard consumes the future shared suite shell/navigation so Relay feels like one utility with Runner and Inspector rather than a separate website. Surface parity means canonical state, actions, receipts, identity and behavioral outcomes remain consistent across inline chat cards, the opened ChatGPT app workspace and relay.loew.fi; it does not require identical composition. VISUAL CANON: the current Inspector chat-card preview gallery is the near-canonical Relay visual language and the dashboard should visibly inherit it: Terra Prime dark surfaces, rounded geometry, Momo display hierarchy, strong feature marks, restrained status color, compact human-first telemetry, and the same spacing/radius/type/icon/token family. The dashboard should feel like that visual system expanded into a persistent workspace, not like a separate redesign. Do not literally stretch inline cards into pages: the web dashboard owns broader navigation, deep links, history, multi-card signal decks, and persistent controls; the opened ChatGPT app may use a denser app-specific workspace; inline cards remain contextual and minimal. Shared components/view-models are encouraged where they preserve each surface's distinct interaction job. No future dashboard redesign should replace the Inspector-preview visual language without explicit owner approval.
queue.next_action: When dashboard work resumes, begin from the current Inspector preview gallery and shared card tokens as the visual reference, then adapt them to workspace-scale navigation and information density rather than inventing a new skin. Preserve the established 2.0 content flows where approved. Treat divergence from the preview language as a review blocker unless explicitly approved.

queue.goal: Document RFS-023 through RFS-033, including feature teams as the canonical organizational layer between assignments and named staff.
queue.acceptance:
Append RFS-023 through RFS-028 to the canonical findings ledger and link each to Relay 1.9 for consideration.

RFS-023 — release-contract propagation friction: umbrella/child requirements currently need manual restatement and can hit acceptance-size/ownership-overlap limits. Consider summarized parent/child contract propagation or reconciliation without stealing ownership.

RFS-024 — live amendment delivery: running chats can miss canonical amendments. Use monotonic consumed-revision cursors and bounded relevant-change checks at safe sync points; no-change injects nothing; scope-changing/blocking updates reconcile before conflicting work.

RFS-025 — caught-up recovery: workers can stop making progress without a true blocker until the user interrupts. Detect no-op/repeated failures/circular replanning/stale progress, recover from canonical checkpoints, state stall point, resume with bounded retries; do not confuse real external waits/auth/client/scope/destructive ambiguity with recoverable stalls.

RFS-026 — recovery learning: validated better capability routes discovered while unsticking work should become reusable guidance. Record constraint, preferred route, fallback, authority boundary and evidence; promote through findings/planning. Example: binary assets prefer binary-capable GitHub transport while Relay retains branch/Runner/PR/deploy/verification authority; UTF-8 base64/chunking is fallback.

RFS-027 — large-asset intake: when GitHub is the better transport, ask the user to upload large/binary files directly to the exact admitted repo/branch/folder with a direct link. Then validate/hash/inspect/rename/move/normalize within scope. Chat transport is fallback.

RFS-028 — workflow-time telemetry: current canonical timestamps support coarse claim→PR/check/merge/wait timing but not reliable active-vs-wait-vs-stall attribution. Add bounded phase/wait/recovery telemetry derived from canonical events/checkpoints. Aggregate by task class, capability/skill, tool family, failure/recovery reason and workflow phase. Staff identity may filter context but never become a productivity score/ranking. Surface recurring bottlenecks and feed validated improvements back into planning/recovery learning.

RFS-029 — executive communication must be implemented as a skill/result contract, not only a narration policy. Normal Relay chat/status should expose a compact human layer (health/outcome, responsible staff, what changed, next step) and keep branches/SHAs/schema/runtime/tool internals in subordinate technical evidence unless they explain a blocker, QA decision or explicit technical request. Add communication-skill guidance, presentation-ready result shaping and eval fixtures that prove technical outputs become plain-language staff-aware updates without losing truth or traceability.

RFS-030 — operational staff routing: Relay has canonical staff identities and assignment roles/taxonomy, but live assignments still require a human to infer who is working on what because staff bindings are not persisted. Add deterministic primary/supporting staff resolution from explicit override + role/category/labels/resources/subnet affinity, persist sticky bindings on the assignment, surface them in staff directory/resume/status, and allow explicit canonical reassignment. Staff identity remains presentation/routing context, never authorization or productivity scoring.
queue.next_action: When branch capacity opens, append RFS-023 through RFS-033 to suggestions.md in one docs-only maintenance change. RFS-033: route assignment -> lowercase feature team -> role -> named staff; preserve sticky home teams plus cross-team memberships; team identity affects routing/presentation, never authorization or productivity scoring. Merge and complete. No Worker deployment.

queue.goal: Eliminate accidental cross-chat work collisions in Relay. Two chats must never be able to silently act as the same active worker on one assignment just because they share the same machine owner or Relay app identity.
queue.acceptance: Runner distinguishes machine/staff ownership from an active chat/workstream lane. Claim/resume issues a bounded opaque lane lease/fencing token to the active chat; canonical assignment state stores only the active lane identity/epoch and heartbeat metadata, not a reusable secret. Assignment mutations and branch-affecting coordination writes require the current lane lease and fail closed with a conflict when called from another chat, even when owner matches. Read-only progress/resume remains available to observers but clearly reports observer/read-only status. Another chat may submit a pending amendment/note without changing live next_action, scope, paths, state or branch; the active lane can accept/reject it. Explicit handoff/takeover rotates the lane epoch/token and records an audit event. Stale lanes may be reclaimed only through an explicit takeover flow with CAS against the latest canonical record. Resume never leaks a current fencing token to a different chat. Tests cover same-owner/different-lane collisions, stale retries, explicit handoff, takeover, observer reads, queued suggestions, and token rotation. Existing path/resource ownership checks remain in force as a second layer.
queue.next_action: Begin immediately after Relay 1.9.9 closes. First document the lane-lease state machine and compatibility path. Then add lane identity/epoch to canonical coordination, require it on assignment mutations, add observer-mode resume/progress, add a pending-amendment inbox for cross-chat suggestions, and implement explicit handoff/takeover with CAS and token rotation. Prove that two simulated chats sharing the same owner cannot mutate the same assignment concurrently.
